prayer.text: Saint Teresa Benedicta (Edith Stein), pray for us.

cues.text: A Philosopher in the Making
Born in 1891 in Breslau, Germany (now Wrocław, Poland), the youngest of eleven children in a devout Jewish family, Edith Stein declared herself an atheist as a teenager.
She entered university, where she studied under the influential philosopher Edmund Husserl at Göttingen.
She became one of his most gifted students and earned her doctorate in philosophy in phenomenology in 1916.
A Conversion Through Reading
Edith's path back toward faith unfolded gradually through her intellectual and personal life.
A visit to Frankfurt Cathedral, where she witnessed an ordinary woman praying quietly, left a deep impression.
Reading the autobiography of St. Teresa of Ávila in a single sitting one summer night convinced her, by her own account, that she had found the truth.
She was baptized into the Catholic Church in 1922.
Barred from Teaching
Edith continued an active academic and lecturing career through the 1920s and early 1930s.
The rise of Nazism and antisemitic legislation forced her resignation from her teaching post in 1933.
Her Jewish ancestry made continued academic work impossible under the new regime, regardless of her Catholic conversion.
Entering Carmel

With her career closed off, Edith entered the Discalced Carmelite convent at Cologne in 1933, after a painful parting from her mother, who never came to understand or accept her daughter's conversion to Christianity.
She took the religious name Teresa Benedicta of the Cross , understanding it as a symbol of her acceptance of suffering to come.
Arrest in the Netherlands

As Nazi persecution intensified, Teresa Benedicta was transferred in 1938 to a Carmelite convent in Echt, in the Netherlands, in hopes of greater safety — a hope the German occupation of Holland in 1940 soon rendered false.
In August 1942, the Gestapo arrested all Catholics of Jewish descent throughout the country.
This was in direct retaliation for a Dutch Catholic bishops' public protest against the deportation of Jews.
Those arrested included Teresa Benedicta and her sister Rosa, who had also become a Carmelite associate.
Legacy
Teresa Benedicta and Rosa were transported to Auschwitz and killed in the gas chambers on August 9, 1942.

Canonized in 1998 by Pope John Paul II , who honored her as 'a daughter of Israel' faithful both to the crucified Christ and to her own Jewish people, she was declared a co-patroness of Europe the following year.
A philosopher and mystic, her death at the hands of the very persecution she had sought refuge from, the Church honors as martyrdom in hatred of the faith.
